title: Quiz: Survival Functions and Kaplan-Meier Estimation

questions.text: The Kaplan-Meier estimator is defined as Ŝ(t) = ∏_{t_i ≤ t} (1 - d_i/n_i). What does n_i represent at event time t_i?
options: The total number of patients enrolled in the study
The number of patients who experienced the event by time t_i
The number of patients still at risk (neither dead nor censored) just before t_i
The number of censored observations up to time t_i
questions.explanation: n_i is the size of the risk set at t_i — the number of patients who have survived (not yet experienced the event) and have not been censored before t_i. This is the denominator in the conditional probability estimate 1 - d_i/n_i. Censored patients leave the risk set at their censoring time, so they correctly contribute information up to the point of censoring.

questions.text: The fundamental identity S(t) = exp(-H(t)) follows from the ODE S'(t) = -h(t)S(t), where H(t) = ∫₀ᵗ h(u) du.
questions.explanation: By definition, h(t) = f(t)/S(t) = -S'(t)/S(t), which gives S'(t) = -h(t)S(t). This separable ODE with S(0)=1 has solution S(t) = exp(-∫₀ᵗ h(u)du) = exp(-H(t)). This identity is foundational: specifying h(t) fully determines S(t) and vice versa.

questions.text: In a study with 50 patients, at time t=100 days there are 40 patients at risk and 3 deaths. What is the KM conditional survival estimate at this time point?
questions.explanation: The term in the KM product at t_i = 100 is (1 - d_i/n_i) = (1 - 3/40) = 37/40 = 0.925. The KM estimate uses n_i (the risk set size at that time point), not the original sample size. The full KM estimate Ŝ(100) is this term multiplied by all previous conditional survival probabilities.

questions.text: A patient is censored at day 200 in a study. How does the KM estimator handle this observation?
options: The patient is excluded from all calculations
The patient is treated as having experienced the event at day 200
The patient remains in the risk set for all event times up to day 200, then is removed
The patient's data is used only to estimate the censoring distribution
questions.explanation: The KM estimator handles censoring by including the patient in the risk set n_i for every event time t_i < 200, then removing them at day 200. They contribute information about surviving to day 200, without incorrectly treating day 200 as a death time. This is why the KM estimator is unbiased under non-informative (independent) censoring.

questions.text: Greenwood's variance formula for the KM estimator is Var(Ŝ(t)) ≈ Ŝ(t)² × ∑_{t_i ≤ t} d_i / [n_i(n_i − d_i)]. If Ŝ(t) = 0.72 and the Greenwood sum is 0.08, what is the approximate 95% CI half-width?
questions.explanation: Var = Ŝ(t)² × Greenwood_sum = 0.72² × 0.08 = 0.5184 × 0.08 = 0.04147. SE = √0.04147 ≈ 0.2036. Half-width = 1.96 × 0.2036 ≈ 0.399. Equivalently, 1.96 × √(Ŝ² × greenwood_sum) = 1.96 × 0.72 × √0.08 ≈ 0.400. Option C is the correct calculation.

questions.text: The log-rank test weights all event times equally, making it most powerful when the hazard ratio between two groups is constant over time (proportional hazards).
questions.explanation: The log-rank test statistic sums (O-E) contributions equally across all event times, giving the greatest power when the hazard ratio is constant — i.e., under proportional hazards. When survival curves cross (non-proportional hazards), or when differences are concentrated early or late, weighted alternatives like the Wilcoxon (rho=1) or Fleming-Harrington tests can be more powerful.
